body:
One-party dominance in a multiparty democracy

After Independence, India adopted a democratic system in which different political parties could contest elections and voters could choose their representatives. However, the Indian National Congress won successive national elections and remained the dominant political party during the first 2 decades.

This situation is called one-party dominance. It must not be confused with a one-party state. In a one-party state, political competition is legally prohibited or severely restricted. In India, opposition parties were permitted to contest elections, organise campaigns and criticise the government. Congress dominance resulted primarily from its electoral strength, organisation and public support.

Why did Congress dominate?

The Congress enjoyed several advantages after Independence:

  • Freedom movement legacy: It had led the national movement and was widely recognised across the country.
  • Nationwide organisation: It had established leaders and party organisations at national, provincial and local levels.
  • Broad social support: Farmers, workers, business groups, different castes and religious communities were represented within its political organisation.
  • Leadership: Jawaharlal Nehru enjoyed considerable public popularity during the early decades.
  • Fragmented opposition: Several opposition parties competed separately, dividing the votes cast against Congress candidates.

The role of the electoral system

India uses the first-past-the-post system for Lok Sabha and State Assembly elections. The candidate receiving the highest number of valid votes in a constituency wins, even without receiving more than 50% of the votes. Consequently, the percentage of seats won by a party need not equal its percentage of votes.

In the 1952 Lok Sabha election, Congress won 364 of 489 seats with approximately 45% of the votes. Its share of seats was much larger than its vote share because opposition votes were distributed among several candidates.

The first 3 general elections

Congress secured decisive Lok Sabha victories in 1952, 1957 and 1962. The Communist Party of India, socialist parties, the Bharatiya Jana Sangh and other organisations nevertheless participated in electoral politics.

Congress dominance was not absolute in every State. In 1957, a Communist-led government headed by E. M. S. Namboodiripad took office in Kerala following Assembly elections. This was an important example of an opposition government emerging through democratic elections while Congress remained dominant nationally.

Why was 1967 a turning point?

The 4th general election of 1967 took place after Nehru's death in 1964 and Lal Bahadur Shastri's death in 1966. Indira Gandhi had become Prime Minister in 1966. During this period, food shortages, drought, rising prices, economic difficulties and disputes within Congress weakened the party's support.

Congress retained its majority in the Lok Sabha, but its position was significantly reduced. At the State level, it lost power in 9 States. Opposition parties formed governments individually or through alliances.

In the then State of Madras, the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam (DMK), led by C. N. Annadurai, defeated Congress and came to power. The result demonstrated the increasing importance of regional political parties.

Coalitions, non-Congressism and defections

Non-Congressism, associated particularly with socialist leader Ram Manohar Lohia, encouraged opposition parties to cooperate electorally against Congress despite their ideological differences.

Several States witnessed Samyukta Vidhayak Dal (SVD) governments. These were alliances of legislators belonging to different parties. A coalition government is formed when more than 1 party participates in governing, generally because no single party can govern independently.

The period also witnessed defections, when elected legislators changed their political allegiance. The expression Aya Ram, Gaya Ram became associated with such changes following the conduct of legislator Gaya Lal in Haryana in 1967.

The 1967 election did not remove Congress from power at the Centre. It weakened Congress's parliamentary position and, more dramatically, ended its control over several State governments.

Prelims focus

  • The first 3 Lok Sabha elections were held in 1952, 1957 and 1962.
  • Congress won 364 of 489 Lok Sabha seats in 1952.
  • The Communist-led government in Kerala took office in 1957 under E. M. S. Namboodiripad.
  • The 4th general election was held in 1967.
  • DMK came to power in Madras in 1967 under C. N. Annadurai.
  • Trap: One-party dominance does not mean that other political parties were prohibited.

[NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India Since Independence, chapter 2, Era of One-Party Dominance, printed pp. 27–38; chapter 5, Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System, printed pp. 84–91. Consulted 23 November 2026.]

title: From Congress Dominance to the Electoral Challenge of 1967

body:
Leadership conflict after 1966

After Lal Bahadur Shastri's death in 1966, Indira Gandhi became Prime Minister with support from influential Congress leaders. Among them was an informal group called the Syndicate, consisting of powerful leaders who exercised considerable influence over the party organisation.

K. Kamaraj was a prominent leader of the Syndicate. Other influential members included S. Nijalingappa, S. K. Patil, Atulya Ghosh and N. Sanjeeva Reddy.

Initially, these leaders expected to exercise influence over government policy and party decisions. Indira Gandhi gradually asserted her independence from them. The disagreement concerned both political authority and the direction of economic policy.

The Presidential election of 1969

The immediate occasion for the Congress split was the 1969 Presidential election, held after President Zakir Husain's death.

The official Congress candidate was N. Sanjeeva Reddy, supported by the Syndicate. V. V. Giri, who was Vice-President, contested as an independent candidate and received Indira Gandhi's support.

Indira Gandhi called for a conscience vote, asking Congress electors to vote according to their judgment rather than follow the party leadership's direction. V. V. Giri won the election. The defeat of the official Congress candidate brought the internal conflict to a decisive stage.

The 2 Congress organisations

In November 1969, Congress formally split into 2 principal groups:

  • Congress (O): O stood for Organisation. This group was associated with the Syndicate.
  • Congress (R): R stood for Requisitionists. This group was led by Indira Gandhi.

The split was presented by Indira Gandhi's supporters as a contest between progressive, pro-poor policies and conservative interests. It also represented a struggle over control of the party.

Economic measures and electoral support

Indira Gandhi sought to strengthen her support among economically disadvantaged sections. Her government nationalised 14 major private banks in 1969. Nationalisation means transferring ownership or control of an enterprise from private owners to the State.

Another major issue was the privy purse, a payment guaranteed to former rulers of princely States as part of the arrangements made during integration. The government attempted to abolish these privileges. Their constitutional abolition was achieved through the 26th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971, not through the 1969 bank nationalisation measure.

The 1971 Lok Sabha election

The split reduced the strength of Indira Gandhi's parliamentary group. She sought a fresh electoral mandate, and the 5th Lok Sabha election was held in 1971.

Major non-communist opposition parties formed a Grand Alliance against her. The opposition campaign was associated with the demand Indira Hatao, meaning removal of Indira Gandhi. Her campaign used the slogan Garibi Hatao, meaning removal of poverty.

Congress (R) won 352 Lok Sabha seats and approximately 44% of the popular vote. Together, Congress (R) and its ally, the Communist Party of India, won 375 seats. This was a decisive restoration of Congress's electoral dominance under Indira Gandhi.

Why was the restored Congress different?

The earlier Congress organisation accommodated numerous influential State leaders and competing internal groups. The Congress that emerged after 1969 was more dependent on the popularity and authority of Indira Gandhi.

Political centralisation in this context means that important decisions concerning leadership, organisation and political strategy increasingly came under the influence of the national leadership rather than being negotiated among powerful State-level factions.

Centralisation strengthened the Prime Minister's authority but reduced the earlier organisation's ability to accommodate different political opinions and interests internally. Electoral dominance was restored, but the organisational structure of the dominant party had changed.

The 1969 split and the 1971 victory are connected but distinct events. The split weakened the old organisational structure; the election subsequently strengthened Indira Gandhi's authority.

Prelims focus

  • The Congress Syndicate was associated with K. Kamaraj and other senior organisational leaders.
  • The main rivals in the 1969 Presidential contest were N. Sanjeeva Reddy and V. V. Giri.
  • Congress (O) meant Organisation; Congress (R) meant Requisitionists.
  • 14 major private banks were nationalised in 1969.
  • Congress (R) won 352 Lok Sabha seats in the 1971 election.
  • Trap: The privy purses were constitutionally abolished in 1971, not in 1969.

[NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India Since Independence, chapter 5, Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System, printed pp. 91–99; Ministry of Law and Justice, Constitution of India, Article 363A, edition as on 10 September 2026. Consulted 23 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Congress conflict led to the 1969 split, Congress (R)'s 352-seat victory in 1971 and greater concentration of party authority around Indira Gandhi.
pictures.caption: Internal conflict transformed the Congress organisation.

title: The Congress Split of 1969 and the Centralisation of Political Leadership

body:
Why did public unrest increase in the 1970s?

Despite the political success of Congress in 1971, India experienced serious economic difficulties during the following years. Rising prices, unemployment, food shortages and dissatisfaction with public administration increased public discontent.

International oil-price increases added to inflation. Poor agricultural conditions in some years also affected food supplies. Students, workers and opposition parties began protesting against rising living costs and alleged corruption.

The Nav Nirman Movement in Gujarat

The Nav Nirman Movement was a major student-led agitation in Gujarat in 1974. Its immediate background was dissatisfaction over rising prices of food and essential commodities and allegations of corruption in government.

Beginning with student protests, the agitation spread across Gujarat and drew support from broader sections of society and opposition parties. It developed from a protest over economic grievances into a movement challenging the State government.

The Congress government in Gujarat fell, and President's Rule was imposed. Under Article 356, President's Rule is a constitutional arrangement used when the government of a State cannot be carried on in accordance with the Constitution. The State's executive authority is exercised through the President, and the State legislature's powers may be exercised by Parliament. It is different from a national Emergency under Article 352.

Following further political pressure, fresh Gujarat Assembly elections were held in June 1975. Congress was defeated, and the opposition-supported Janata Morcha emerged victorious.

The Gujarat Assembly election of June 1975 took place before the national Emergency was declared on 25 June 1975.

The Bihar Movement of 1974

In March 1974, students in Bihar protested against rising prices, unemployment, food scarcity and corruption. The agitation subsequently invited veteran socialist and Gandhian leader Jayaprakash Narayan, widely known as JP, to provide leadership.

JP agreed to lead the movement on the condition that it should be non-violent and should not remain limited to Bihar. He called for Sampoorna Kranti, or Total Revolution.

Total Revolution referred to extensive change in political, social and economic life. JP argued that democratic reform required more than replacing one government with another. His movement called for action against corruption and improvements in public life.

The Railway Strike of 1974

In May 1974, railway employees organised a nationwide strike under the leadership of George Fernandes. The workers demanded improvements in service conditions and related benefits.

The strike disrupted a major national transport system and became an important example of labour unrest during this period. It was eventually called off without a settlement after strong government action.

The Allahabad High Court judgment of June 1975

Political tension increased sharply after a judgment of the Allahabad High Court on 12 June 1975. Justice Jagmohan Lal Sinha declared Indira Gandhi's 1971 Lok Sabha election invalid following an election petition filed by socialist leader Raj Narain.

The judgment concerned electoral malpractice, including the use of government assistance in the election campaign. On 24 June 1975, the Supreme Court granted a conditional interim stay pending further consideration of the case.

Opposition leaders demanded Indira Gandhi's resignation. On 25 June 1975, JP addressed a major opposition gathering at Ramlila Maidan in Delhi. Later that day, the constitutional Emergency provisions were invoked.

The court judgment was an important immediate political trigger, but it did not itself require the declaration of a national Emergency.

Mahagujarat Movement: A linguistic Statehood movement associated with the creation of Gujarat in 1960.
Nav Nirman Movement: A student-led movement against price rises and corruption in Gujarat in 1974.

Prelims focus

  • Nav Nirman was a major student-led agitation in Gujarat in 1974.
  • The Bihar Movement began in March 1974 and was led by Jayaprakash Narayan.
  • Sampoorna Kranti means Total Revolution.
  • George Fernandes led the nationwide Railway Strike in May 1974.
  • Justice Jagmohan Lal Sinha delivered the Allahabad High Court judgment on 12 June 1975.
  • Trap: Gujarat's Nav Nirman Movement and the Mahagujarat Movement were different movements with different objectives.

[NCERT, Class 12, Politics in India Since Independence, chapter 6, The Crisis of Democratic Order, printed pp. 102–109; chapter 5, Challenges to and Restoration of the Congress System, printed pp. 86–89; Ministry of Law and Justice, Constitution of India, Articles 352 and 356, edition as on 10 September 2026. Consulted 23 November 2026.]
